slides.title: Plan for the day

slides.title: Criteria for identifying a cell
bullets: Compare the size of the leukocyte with red cells and note its shape.
Assess the shape, structure and size of the nucleus relative to the whole cell, the density of the nucleus and its position (central or at the edge).
Note the appearance and colour of the cytoplasm and of all granules.
Determine the nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio.
Check whether any vacuoles are present (stained or unstained).
Learn to recognise normal cells correctly — then you will be able to detect abnormal leukocytes.

slides.title: Normal leukocytes: neutrophils and lymphocytes
rows: 2–5 lobes joined by thin strands; chromatin dark violet
Abundant, slightly pink; fine pink-violet granules
Horseshoe-, band- or ring-shaped, not divided into lobes; edges serrated

slides.title: Normal leukocytes: neutrophils and lymphocytes
rows: Oval or round, may be pushed to one side
Abundant, pale blue; a few large dark red granules
Large, usually fills the whole cell; chromatin dark violet and dense
Very scanty, blue, usually without granules

slides.title: Normal leukocytes: monocyte, eosinophil, basophil
rows: Smoky grey-blue; large and small vacuoles may be present
Packed with granules; large red-orange granules cover most of the cell

slides.title: Normal leukocytes: monocyte, eosinophil, basophil
rows: The nucleus is hard to see because of the granules

slides.title: Normal leukocytes (photographs)
slides.caption: White blood cell at the centre (neutrophil): white cells are typically seen in a peripheral blood smear. Neutrophils are a type of white cell and one of the body's main defences against infection; finding them in a smear is normal. Numerous red blood cells: they carry oxygen from the lungs to the tissues and return carbon dioxide to the lungs.
slides.credit: Photo: Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya, CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

slides.title: Normal leukocytes (photographs)
slides.caption: Many red cells in a smear are normal; a high number may be linked to polycythaemia or dehydration. Platelets (dot-like bodies): small cell fragments involved in clotting and wound healing, seen as small dots. A normal platelet number is essential for clotting; low counts (thrombocytopenia) or abnormal function can cause bleeding disorders.
slides.credit: Photo: Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya, CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

slides.title: Neutrophils
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: %, ×10⁹/L

What it is used for: This value is part of the blood differential, which measures the amount and/or percentage of each type of white blood cell. Because the five types do different jobs, measuring them separately gives important information. The test is ordered at routine checkups, to find the cause of symptoms (such as unusual tiredness, weakness or unexplained bruising) or of an abnormal WBC count on another test, and to monitor an existing blood disorder; it helps diagnose infections, autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, leukemia and other cancers.

slides.title: Neutrophils
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Neutrophils are the most common type of white blood cell and the body’s main defense against infection when bacteria, viruses or other germs enter the body; they mostly target bacterial infections.
slides.credit: Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Neutrophils
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result · 1/2
cols: A higher-than-normal amount of neutrophils is known as neutrophilia.
A lower-than-normal amount of neutrophils is known as neutropenia.
Some cancers and treatments such as chemotherapy lower white cell counts and raise infection risk: at times in the treatment cycle neutrophils are particularly low.

slides.title: Neutrophils
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result · 2/2
cols: Blood tests check for neutropenia during treatment; signs of infection (such as a fever of 38 °C or higher) need urgent care.

slides.title: Neutrophils, Monocytes, Eosinophils, Basophils
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for a blood differential.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.
Interferences: Blood differential results can be affected by physical injury or extreme stress, smoking and alcohol use; an abnormal result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.

slides.title: Neutrophils, Monocytes, Eosinophils, Basophils
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Limitations: If results seem abnormal, the provider may order other tests to find the cause; symptoms, medical history and other blood test results are considered.

slides.title: Lymphocytes
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: %, ×10⁹/L

Physiology: Lymphocytes include two main types: B cells and T cells. B cells fight off invading viruses, bacteria or toxins; certain T cells target and destroy the body’s own cells, such as cancer cells and virus-infected cells.
Lymphocytes mostly target viral infections.

slides.title: Lymphocytes
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
cols: A higher-than-normal amount of lymphocytes is known as lymphocytosis.
A lower-than-normal amount of lymphocytes is known as lymphopenia.

slides.title: Lymphocytes
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for a blood differential.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.
Interferences: Blood differential results can be affected by physical injury or extreme stress, smoking and alcohol use; an abnormal result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.

slides.title: Lymphocytes
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Limitations: CD4 cells (“helper T cells”) are a type of lymphocyte that HIV attacks and destroys. A separate test — the CD4 count — is used to check the immune system in people with HIV.
If results seem abnormal, the provider may order other tests to find the cause; symptoms, medical history and other blood test results are considered.

slides.title: Monocytes
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: %, ×10⁹/L
Physiology: Monocytes kill bacteria, viruses and other germs that may cause illness. They also boost the body’s immune response and clear away dead cells.

slides.title: Eosinophils
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: %, ×10⁹/L
Physiology: Eosinophils defend against parasites and infections, are involved in allergies and help control inflammation (swelling and redness).

Normally the blood does not have a large number of eosinophils. In some conditions they move out of the bloodstream and build up in organs and tissues such as the esophagus, heart, lungs and intestines, causing inflammation.

slides.title: Eosinophils
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: The body may produce more eosinophils in response to allergic disorders, skin conditions, parasitic and fungal infections, autoimmune diseases, some cancers and bone marrow disorders.

slides.title: Basophils
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: %, ×10⁹/L
Physiology: Basophils release enzymes during allergic reactions and asthma attacks.

slides.title: Segmented neutrophil
slides.caption:
Size: 12–15 µm
Nucleus: 2–5 lobes joined by thin chromatin strands; deep purple
Cytoplasm: Abundant, pale pink
Granules: Very small, numerous, mauve
Key feature: Thin “thread” between lobes — that makes it segmented.
slides.credit: Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Band neutrophil
slides.caption:
Size: Not given separately (immature granulocytes: 12–18 µm)
Nucleus: Not divided into lobes: an elongated, curved band (C or S shape)
Cytoplasm: Pale pink, as in a segmented neutrophil
Granules: Fine, mauve
slides.credit: Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Band neutrophil
slides.caption:
Key feature: No lobes separated by a thin strand.
Seen in: Increased in infections and myelodysplasia; in Pelger–Huët anomaly nuclear shape is altered congenitally.
slides.credit: Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Small lymphocyte
slides.caption:
Size: 7–10 µm
Nucleus: Round, fills most of the cell; dense, dark chromatin
Cytoplasm: Scant — a thin blue rim
Granules: None
Key feature: A little larger than a red cell, almost all nucleus.
slides.credit: Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Large lymphocyte
slides.caption:
Size: 10–15 µm
Nucleus: Round or oval, may lie to one side
Cytoplasm: More abundant, clear pale blue
Granules: May have a few large dark-red (azurophilic) granules
Key feature: Clear blue cytoplasm, no vacuoles or dust-like granules.
slides.credit: Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Monocyte
slides.caption:
Size: 15–25 µm — the largest leukocyte
Nucleus: Variable, often kidney-shaped; pale chromatin in strands
Cytoplasm: Grey-blue; vacuoles usually present
Granules: Fine, dust-like, reddish
Key feature: Large + pale folded nucleus + grey “ground-glass” cytoplasm.
slides.credit: Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Monocyte
slides.caption: Seen in: In malaria, brown-black pigment may be seen in the cytoplasm.
slides.credit: Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Eosinophil
slides.caption:
Size: 12–15 µm
Nucleus: Usually 2 lobes (“spectacles”)
Cytoplasm: Barely visible because of the granules
Granules: Large, round, densely packed, orange-red
Key feature: Large orange-red granules — no other cell has this colour.
slides.credit: Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Eosinophil
slides.caption: Seen in: Sometimes the cell is damaged with scattered granules.
slides.credit: Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Basophil
slides.caption:
Size: 11–13 µm
Nucleus: Hard to see — covered by granules
Cytoplasm: Barely visible; sometimes small colourless vacuoles
Granules: Very large, deep purple; less densely packed than in eosinophils
Key feature: The rarest granulocyte; granules cover the nucleus too.
slides.credit: Schematic (not a photomicrograph)
